BillingAccountOut.description:
The account screen's view of a plan (FR-48).

**The wider read `SubscriptionOut` deliberately refused to become.** That schema stays
one bool because *"a field here would be a field two callers could disagree about"*;
this one carries the state a person needs to act on their own subscription, and the two
cannot disagree because `is_pro` here is computed from the same
`LIVE_SUBSCRIPTION_STATUSES` the entitlement read uses.

**`needs_payment` is the field this schema exists for.** `is_pro` is true for a
`past_due` account — a failed payment leaves someone entitled while they fix it — so a
screen that could only see the bool would show a person with a recoverable problem
exactly what it shows a person with none.

**`period_end` is not a renewal date**, and is not named as one. This product does not
model `cancel_at_period_end`, so a subscription cancelled in the provider's portal reads
`active` until its term runs out and nothing here can tell them apart. The field says
when the current term ends, which is true in both cases.
BillingAccountOut.title: BillingAccountOut

BrowseCardOut.description:
One Browse card (FR-26): public facts, the personal explanation, and save state.

**`tags` are Why-this Tags — the Relevance Pulse, not the Event Fit.** AD-10 forbids
substituting one explanation for the other, and this surface is authed: its first
section head says "3 worth your attention today". The tags and the confidence come
from the same `RankingInputs` the ranking used, so the explanation cannot drift from
the decision.

**`is_saved` is on the card, not in an envelope-level set.** The Save button's initial
state is a property of the card, and an already-saved event must render "Saved ✓" on
first paint rather than flashing "Save" — which a client-side join invites.

**`stripe` is capped server-side.** At most one card per response carries `must_know`.
A client-side cap would be per page, so two pages would each show "their one" and the
surface as a whole would flood.
BrowseCardOut.title: BrowseCardOut

BrowseOut.description:
The Browse surface for the signed-in user (FR-26, FR-48).

**Every state answers 200.** A user with no city, a city with nothing on this week,
and an offset past the end are all answers rather than errors — the client tells them
apart by `city_missing` and `total`, and tells all three from a failure by the fact
that a failure is not a 200 at all. That distinction is the whole reason the surface
can say "Nothing matched." and "Nothing nearby tonight." and mean different things.

**`total` is the size of the ranked pool, not a `COUNT(*)`.** It is what the user can
actually page to. A count taken in SQL would include events that FR-14's staleness
bound — applied in Python, because it is per source — then drops, so the section head
would advertise a number no amount of scrolling reaches.

**`tier_2_starts_at` is the server's.** The two section heads are "3 worth your
attention today" and "More this week", and the rule that splits them lives here so it
cannot drift from the Digest's idea of what is worth attention.
BrowseOut.title: BrowseOut

BrowseQuotaOut.description:
What the user's save allowance stands at — for showing, never for deciding.

**This is read without spending it.** The gate (`check_save_allowed`) counts an
attempt by contract, so asking *it* what the allowance is would charge a user a save
for loading a page. The read goes through `ThrottlePort.peek`, which counts nothing.

**A Pro account has `cap: null`,** not a very large number. FR-48's consequence is
that a Pro user has no soft wall at all, and a cap of "infinity" is a number a client
would eventually render into the hero.
BrowseQuotaOut.title: BrowseQuotaOut

CalendarCapDetails.description:
The `details` of a calendar-cap refusal: the cap, and one upgrade sentence.

**Exactly two fields, and nothing else** — the same shape as `SaveCapDetails`, and
for the same reason. No `modal`, no `title`, no `actions`, no `dismissable`: the
refusal is an *inline* prompt with a quiet "Upgrade" link, not a modal
(EXPERIENCE.md §3, the Free-tier cap prompt). A cap that interrupts with a modal is a
cap that trains people to dismiss prompts.

The two tier caps — one on connected calendars, one on saves — therefore speak **one**
language to the frontend: a number and a sentence. The frontend renders one prompt
component for both.
CalendarCapDetails.title: CalendarCapDetails

CalendarCapOut.description:
The 409 a refused calendar connection answers with (FR-50).

**A conflict, not a bad request.** The address the user pasted is perfectly good — it
is the *state of the account* that refuses it, because the account already holds as
many calendars as its plan allows. The request was well-formed and conflicts with the
account, which is what a 409 means.

This is the only 409 the connect route can answer, so it needs no union — unlike the
save route, which refuses for two different reasons.
CalendarCapOut.title: CalendarCapOut

CalendarConnectIn.description:
A provider and the secret address to connect.

The `address` is the secret ICS/webcal address. It is **write-only**: it goes in
and it is never handed back, in whole or in part, in any response.
CalendarConnectIn.title: CalendarConnectIn

CalendarConnectionOut.description:
One calendar connection, as it is shown to the user.

There is no `address` field and no `fingerprint` field. The fingerprint is a keyed
HMAC and so is not a secret, but it is not the user's business either, and a digest
in a response body is one more thing to leak in a screenshot.

`last_error_kind` is a **slug** (`revoked`, `transient`, …), never a message and
never a URL: an `httpx` exception message contains the full request URL, which *is*
the credential (AD-13).
CalendarConnectionOut.title: CalendarConnectionOut

CalendarReconnectIn.description:
A new address for a connection the provider revoked.

The provider revoked the old secret, so the address the user pastes now is a *new*
one. The connection's row is reused rather than a second row being created.
CalendarReconnectIn.title: CalendarReconnectIn

CategoryMuteIn.description: The request body for setting one category mute.
CategoryMuteIn.title: CategoryMuteIn

CategoryMuteListOut.description:
Every active category mute for the signed-in user.

**An expired mute is not in the list.** The row is still there — it is the user's
data — but it no longer mutes anything, so the screen does not list it.
CategoryMuteListOut.title: CategoryMuteListOut

CategoryMuteOut.description: One active category mute, as the settings screen reads it.
CategoryMuteOut.title: CategoryMuteOut

CategoryMuteRestoreDefaultsOut.description:
The outcome of the bulk reset.

**`removed` is how many mutes were cleared**, so the screen can say what happened
rather than just that it happened.
CategoryMuteRestoreDefaultsOut.title: CategoryMuteRestoreDefaultsOut

CategoryMuteResultOut.description:
The outcome of setting or clearing one category mute.

**`changed` says whether the call did anything.** Setting a mute that is already set
is a success, not an error — but a response claiming a change when none happened
would make the screen redraw something that did not move.
CategoryMuteResultOut.title: CategoryMuteResultOut

CheckoutIn.description:
The checkout request: which plan to buy.

**The plan is the only field.** There is deliberately no `success_url`, no
`cancel_url` and no `return_url`, and that absence is the security property rather
than an oversight: the URLs handed to the provider are built from configuration, so a
client cannot name one. Taking the redirect target from the request is the classic
open-redirect in a checkout flow — a crafted target sends a paying user (and the
session id in the query string) to somebody else's site.

The plan is an enum, so an unknown one is a 422 at the edge rather than a provider
error later.
CheckoutIn.title: CheckoutIn

CheckoutOut.description:
The checkout answer: the URL to send the user to.

**It carries no entitlement, and asking for one here would be a lie.** The user is not
Pro when this response is written; they are Pro when the provider's webhook lands,
which may be later or never. So there is no `is_pro` field, no status and no plan
echo: the answer is a URL and nothing else.
CheckoutOut.title: CheckoutOut

CityPageEventOut.description:
One event on a city page.

**The score and the tags are the persisted Event Fit, served as stored** (AD-10).
The page shows what the fit says, not what a fresh computation would say — so a
score of 1 on an event that would now score 5 is shown as 1, and the reason is that
the fit has not been recomputed yet.
CityPageEventOut.title: CityPageEventOut

CityPageOut.description:
One city page: the city's identity, its events, and whether it is published.

**`is_published` is FR-27's threshold, computed by the listing's own filters.** A
city with more than the threshold's events is published; a city with fewer is not,
and the frontend renders "coming soon" rather than a listing. **The city page
degrades; it does not 404** — a URL that vanishes after ranking throws away every
bit of ranking it earned.

**`event_count` is the qualifying count**, not the number of items on this page. It
is the number the threshold was decided on. `has_next` is measured against the
**listing's** total instead — the two counts answer different questions, and a city
between seasons has the first without the second.
CityPageOut.title: CityPageOut

CityPageQuery.description:
The city page endpoint's query parameters.

**`page` and `page_size` are bounded at the edge, and the edge is a refusal.**
A page below one or a page size above the ceiling is a **422**, not a silent
adjustment — a caller that asks for 10,000 events a page has made a mistake, and
quietly handing it 50 would hide the mistake from it.

The service below the surface **clamps** rather than refuses, because it is also
called directly by code that is not an HTTP request and should not raise a
validation error. The two layers answer the same question in the way that suits
each: a bad request is refused, a bad internal call is bounded.
CityPageQuery.title: CityPageQuery

CollectionEventOut.description:
One saved event inside a collection — **the snapshot, and only the snapshot**.

**This deliberately carries no title, venue or URL**, which is what makes it different
from `SavedEventOut`. Those fields are the catalog's current values, read at request
time; reading them here would put a `catalog` query behind a `personal` endpoint, and
AD-3 forbids relating the two. The snapshot is what AD-17 propagation keeps correct and
what the Timeline and the conflict detector already use, so it is what this returns.

A surface that wants titles has `GET /api/personal/saved-events`, which is the endpoint
that owns that join.
CollectionEventOut.title: CollectionEventOut

CollectionIn.description:
The body of a create or a rename: a name, and nothing else (FR-49).

**No position.** Where a new collection lands is the server's rule — the end — and a
client that could choose would be a second writer of an ordering the reorder endpoint
already owns. Moving one is what `PUT /collections/order` is for.
CollectionIn.title: CollectionIn

CollectionOrderIn.description:
A whole ordering, in one request (FR-49).

**The complete list, never a move instruction.** "Put this one third" has to be
interpreted against a list that may have changed since the client read it; a complete
order is unambiguous, and the result is the order the user saw themselves arrange. The
command refuses a list that does not name every collection exactly once, so the server
never observes a partially reordered list.
CollectionOrderIn.title: CollectionOrderIn

CollectionOut.description:
One collection as the client sees it.

`item_count` is here because every surface that lists collections wants it, and a
client counting for itself would need the membership of each one — turning one list
into N requests.
CollectionOut.title: CollectionOut

ConflictListOut.description:
The user's conflict pairs, split into what needs a decision and what is history.

`resolved` holds exactly the pairs **the user answered**. A pair that was closed
because a side went away — `cleared_by_state_change` — is neither list's business:
nobody chose it, so it is not the user's history to read.
ConflictListOut.title: ConflictListOut

ConflictListSideOut.description:
One side of a pair, as the conflict list hands it over.

**`name` is nullable, and `available` says why.** A side whose record cannot be read
has no title to show. The client renders "event no longer available" rather than a
blank name, so the state is explicit instead of looking like an event with no title.

A side is unavailable when its own row is gone, or — for a saved side — when the
catalog no longer **publishes** the event. The catalog's published interface is the
only view across the schema wall (AD-2 / AD-3), and an event that is unpublished, in
review or superseded is simply not in it. This is the same rule `GET
/api/personal/saved-events` follows.

`start_time_tz` is the side's **display** zone: the personal event's own zone, or the
catalog event's zone for a saved side. It is None for an unavailable side, because the
snapshot is UTC and the display zone is then genuinely unknown.
ConflictListSideOut.title: ConflictListSideOut

ConflictOut.description:
One conflict the user must answer.

`actions` is the closed set of three choices for this conflict's kind **and the side
the user just acted on**. `dismiss` is not among them and cannot be expressed.

**Both sides are named.** The 409 is the client's route to a resolution, and a
resolution names a side — so the client needs the side it just created or saved, and
the side it clashes with, each with its kind. `new_side` is the one the user just
touched; `other_side` is the one it clashes with.
ConflictOut.title: ConflictOut

ConflictPairOut.description:
One pair, with both sides and the choices it offers.

**Both sides are present, symmetrically.** The pair row stores them sorted, so the row
cannot say which side the user should move — the resolve flow decides that, by the
action the user picks.

`actions` is the allowed set for an **active** pair, and it comes from the service's
maps — the same ones the resolve endpoint enforces, so there is one source and not a
second list. A **resolved** pair carries no actions (there is nothing left to choose)
and instead carries `resolution` and `resolved_at`.

**A pair with a saved side offers four actions.** The list presents both sides
symmetrically and does not know which one the user will act on, so it offers the
union across the pair's sides: `delete_new` for the personal side, `skip_public` for
the saved one, and the two shared choices. A personal-vs-personal pair is unaffected —
its union is exactly the three it has always offered.
ConflictPairOut.title: ConflictPairOut

ConflictResolutionIn.description:
The body of a resolution: which action, and which side it is about.

**`side` names the side the action applies to**, and it carries the kind as well as
the id. The pair row is **symmetric** — it stores both sides sorted — so the row
cannot say which side the user is acting on, and the request has to.

The field is called `side` rather than `new_side` because "new" is only true of the
prompt: for a pair reviewed later on `/conflicts` there is no new side, there are two
sides and the user picks one.

**The kind is what makes the request safe.** The action decides what it may act on:
`delete_new` deletes a personal event and refuses a saved side; `skip_public`
releases a save and refuses a personal side. So a client cannot delete a personal
event by naming a saved side, and it cannot release somebody else's save by naming a
personal one. The rule is per-action, which is what it has to be now that both kinds
of side are answerable.
ConflictResolutionIn.title: ConflictResolutionIn

ConflictResolutionOut.description:
The outcome of a resolution.

`action_side` is the side the action was about — the client opens it in edit mode for
`edit_new`, or finds it already deleted for `delete_new`, or finds the save gone for
`skip_public`. `other_side` is the pair's other side.

Both carry their kind, which the old shape did not: the old `new_side_id` was always
a personal event, so the kind was implied.
ConflictResolutionOut.title: ConflictResolutionOut

ConflictSideOut.description:
One side of a conflict: the event that clashes.

The times are UTC instants. The side does not carry a timezone of its own — the sides
are two records that may live in two different zones, and a conflict is about the
instants they occupy, not about how either is displayed.

`kind` says which kind of record this side names: a personal event the user owns, or
a save of a public event. The client needs it to post a resolution — the resolution
names the side, and the side is a `(kind, id)` pair.
ConflictSideOut.title: ConflictSideOut

ConflictSideRef.description:
The side a resolution acts on: its kind and its id.

The pair row stores its two sides **by value** as `(kind, id)` — the kind beside the
id, because the id is a UUID and a UUID does not say what it points at. This is that
same shape, so the server can check the request against the row without a
translation.
ConflictSideRef.title: ConflictSideRef

CsrfTokenOut.description:
The CSRF token the frontend sends back on every unsafe request.

The token is also set as the `csrftoken` cookie on the same response; the frontend
reads the cookie and echoes the value in the `X-CSRFToken` header. Sending both is
Django's own convention, and it is the one `CsrfViewMiddleware` checks.
CsrfTokenOut.title: CsrfTokenOut

CurrentUserOut.description:
The signed-in user.

The id and the email are what the frontend needs. There is no password field, no
permission field and no catch-all, so nothing internal can ride along.

The **onboarding status** is here, and it is here because the frontend needs it to
decide between the onboarding flow and the home. It says only whether the onboarding
is finished and which step the user is on — it carries no interests and no digest
preference, because `me` is about *who* the user is and a settings blob there would
grow without bound. The full state lives at `/api/personal/onboarding`.

The **name** is here for the same reason the email is: the frontend shows it on
every screen, so it is a read the frontend already makes. It is `""` when no name is
set — the one "no name set" state — and the frontend renders its own email-derived
fallback in that case. **The backend does not guess a name from an address**: how a
human renders their own name is a display concern, not a stored one.

It is read through `personalization`'s **published interface** — the service, never
the model — because `identity` may not reach into another app's tables (AD-2). The
import contract `models-personalization` proves it.
CurrentUserOut.title: CurrentUserOut

DataExportOut.description:
One export request, as the settings screen sees it.

**It carries no download links.** The links live in the email, which is what FR-52
promises and what keeps a session-authed response from becoming a second way to reach
a file that is supposed to require the token.
DataExportOut.title: DataExportOut

DetailConflictOut.description:
The caller's **active** conflict pair for this event (FR-33, FR-58).

**The screen knows which event it is showing**, so this is not a symmetric pair —
it is the pair's *other* side, the one the save clashes with. The client does not
have to work out which of two sides is "mine".

**Both sides are named, because a resolution names a side.** The request body
(`ConflictResolutionIn.side`) carries a `(kind, id)` pair, and the server checks it
against the pair's own two sides — so the client has to be able to name the side it
is acting on. `saved_side` is the **save row's** id, which is *not* the catalog
event's id: the pair stores a `SavedEvent` by that row's id, and `skip_public`
releases the save by the same id. `other_side` is the personal event's id. Without
both, the client would have to guess an id, and a guessed id is refused by the server.

**`actions` is the saved side's set**, not the pair's union. The Detail Screen acts
on the save — "skip this event" releases it — so the choices are `keep_both`,
`edit_new` and `skip_public`. The union would also offer `delete_new`, and deleting
the user's personal event is not a choice this surface should present.

**Only an active pair is here.** A resolved pair is history and a cleared one is
nobody's decision; neither means "there is a choice waiting".
DetailConflictOut.title: DetailConflictOut

DetailConflictSideOut.description:
The side a saved event clashes with, as the Detail Screen reads it.

**`name` is nullable**, for the same reason the conflict list's side is: a side
whose record has gone has no title to show, and the client renders "event no longer
available" rather than a blank. `ConflictSideOut` — the 409's shape — requires a
name, because the 409 names a side the user just touched, and that one is always
there.

**No timezone of its own.** The side is a record that may live in a different zone
from the event on screen, and a conflict is about the instants they occupy.
DetailConflictSideOut.title: DetailConflictSideOut

DetailNoticeOut.description:
The newest state-change notice for this event, as the Detail banner shows it.

**It is the newest notice for this event, regardless of dismissal.** That is the
deliberate rule of `delivery.services.notice_state`: the banner is about *this* event,
which the user has navigated to on purpose, so dismissing the strip on the digest home
must not hide "this event was cancelled" from the event's own page.

**`dismissed_at` says whether the user has already closed it.** The banner renders
that state rather than pretending the correction never happened — the notice is still
the truth about this event, and the user may still want to read it.

**`seen_at` is when it was first put in front of them** — not an act by them, and
not the same thing as the dismissal. The two are separate columns on the row and
they are separate fields here. (Today a dismissal sets both; the strip's read
deliberately does not mark notices seen, because a `GET` that writes is the shape
CSRF exists to stop.)

**No `event_id`.** The Detail read is already scoped to one event and the response's
enclosing `event` object names it. A redundant field could disagree with its own
parent.
DetailNoticeOut.title: DetailNoticeOut

DetailPersonalOut.description:
The signed-in user's own state for an event (FR-24, FR-54, FR-55).

**Five independent facts, and none of them implies another.** "There is no
explanation" and "you have not saved this" are different, and a client that cannot
tell them apart renders the wrong thing. The same is true of the two newest ones:
**a notice and a mute are different facts**, and a client must not read "muted" as
"there is nothing to say".

**`why_this` is `None` when no composition exists** for this `(user, event)` pair.
That is an **explicit absence**: not an empty breakdown, not a zero bucket, and not
a recomputed one. AD-10 says the screen "renders no explanation rather than
recomputing one if none exists".
DetailPersonalOut.title: DetailPersonalOut

DigestCardOut.description:
One Pulse Card on the digest (FR-6).

**The bucket, not the score.** FR-22's raw `relevance_score` is an internal number;
the card shows 1-5 dots. Sending the score would invite the frontend to re-bucket it
— which is the "recomputed at render" failure wearing a different hat, and would break
the no-flicker rule, since the bucket the user saw this morning is a **persisted fact
about their day**. The Detail Screen's own read carries the score; the card's
contract is the card's.

**The tags are the persisted keys, in the persisted order.** They are not recomputed
and not re-sorted — the order is the priority order, and it is what the card and the
Detail Screen must agree on (AD-10). The client owns the labels.

**The times are instants plus the IANA zone.** AD-6: "display-time conversion happens
at the presentation edge, never in domain logic". The API does not send a
pre-formatted local string.

**The display facts are optional.** They live in the catalog (for a public event) or
in the user's own agenda (for a personal one), and either place may have moved on
since the composition. When they have, `catalog_event_missing` says so and the
*explanation* is still there — the composition is a fact about the day, and its
explanation must not change because a source moved.

**`source_badge` is the variant key, or `None`.** A personal event has no source, so
it has no badge; `None` here means "there is no source", not "unknown". The client
owns the label and the glyph.
DigestCardOut.title: DigestCardOut

DigestOut.description:
The signed-in user's Pulse Digest for their local day (FR-5, FR-8, FR-6).

**`status` says which of the three states this is**, and all three answer **200**.
A 404 would mean "there is no such digest", which is true of `not_composed` and false
of `empty` — and the client would have to map a status code onto "nothing happening"
versus "not ready", which is exactly the interpretation the API is supposed to
remove.

**The city carries its `city_source`,** because the fallback city is not the user's
city: FR-8's copy is "No qualifying events in **{city}**", and if the city is the
server's fallback rather than the user's, the copy is misleading.

**`timezone` is on the response.** The digest row stores the zone it was composed in,
and the client needs it to render the local date it was given. Without it, a client
showing "Wednesday" has no way to know which Wednesday.
DigestOut.title: DigestOut

DigestPreferenceIn.description:
The digest delivery time and timezone, and the two content preferences.

The delivery time is a **local wall clock** — "09:00" means nine in the morning where
the user is, not nine in the morning UTC. The zone says where that is.

**The two new fields are optional, and omission means "leave it alone".** The city
and the opt-out are separate settings, and a client that only wants to change the
delivery time must not silently clear the city or silently re-include personal
events.

**`city` is the user's home city, in the catalog's spelling.** A city the catalog
does not cover is stored as the fallback with `city_source` `fallback`, so the digest
can say "we don't have your city yet" rather than passing the fallback off as the
user's city.

**A `null` city is not a clearing, and this endpoint cannot clear.** A `null` and an
omitted field are the same value here, so "leave it alone" and "clear it" cannot be
told apart — and a shape that cannot say which one it means must not guess. Guessing
"clear" would wipe the city of every client that sends the field as `null`, and
guessing "leave alone" would make the value unreachable. So a `null` city is
**left alone**, and clearing is not offered here at all: the service can clear the
city (`set_home_city(city=None)`), and a future settings endpoint may expose it
through a shape that *can* distinguish the two. Until then, "no city" is reached by
the sign-up path or by the backfill, not by this request.
DigestPreferenceIn.title: DigestPreferenceIn

DigestPreferenceOut.description:
The stored digest delivery time and timezone, and the two content preferences.

`city_source` says how the city was arrived at — `geo`, `choice`, `fallback` or
`backfill`. A client can show "we don't have your city yet" for a fallback rather
than implying New York City is the user's city.
DigestPreferenceOut.title: DigestPreferenceOut

DigestScheduleIn.description:
The digest delivery time and the zone it is a clock in.

**Both or neither.** A wall clock without its zone is not a schedule, so the two cannot
be changed apart and cannot be half-applied.

delivery_time.description: When the daily digest is due, as a local wall clock.
delivery_time.title: Delivery Time

timezone.description: The IANA zone the delivery time is a clock in.
timezone.title: Timezone

DigestScheduleIn.title: DigestScheduleIn

DigestScheduleOut.description:
When and where the daily digest is due.

`delivery_time` is a **local wall clock** — "09:00" means nine in the morning where the
user is — and `timezone` is the IANA zone it is a clock in. They are one object because
they are one fact: a clock without its zone is not a schedule.
DigestScheduleOut.title: DigestScheduleOut

DismissalIn.description:
The request body for recording one dismissal.

**Only the event id is needed.** The slot is *read*, not sent: the service resolves
it from the user's own composition, so a client cannot claim a dismissal came from a
slot it did not come from — and cannot put a serendipity card into the cluster by
asserting it did.
DismissalIn.title: DismissalIn

DismissalOut.description:
What one dismissal did.

**`cluster_advanced` says whether this dismissal counted**, and `prompt_due` says
whether the product should now ask. Both are separate facts: a dismissal that
advanced the counter may still not have completed a cluster, and a dismissal that did
not advance can never complete one.
DismissalOut.title: DismissalOut

EffectiveQuietHoursOut.description:
One weekday of the schedule the delivery path will actually use (FR-51).

**Read-only, and derived.** It is the base window with a Pro account's overrides laid
over it; for a Free or lapsed account it is the base window on all seven days whatever
`quiet_hours_overrides` holds. It exists so a lapsed user is never shown seven windows
that are not in force — the one honest answer to "when will I actually be quiet".

`quiet_hours` is `null` on a day with no quiet hours at all.
EffectiveQuietHoursOut.title: EffectiveQuietHoursOut

EventDetailFactsOut.description:
The event's public facts, as the Detail Screen shows them.

**These are the catalog's own fields**, read through the published read interface.
The description is the *stripped* field — `formats.text.plain_text` removed the
markup, decoded the entities and truncated it before it was stored — so it is
display content, not raw source payload (AD-9).

**The times are instants plus the IANA zone.** AD-6: "display-time conversion happens
at the presentation edge, never in domain logic".
EventDetailFactsOut.title: EventDetailFactsOut

EventDetailOut.description:
One event's Detail Screen (FR-24).

**The public facts are the catalog's,** read through `catalog_read`'s published
interface — never from `apps.ingestion.models` directly, and never through the
Event Fit.

**`personal` is `None` for an anonymous caller.** It is `None` rather than an empty
`DetailPersonalOut` because "you are not signed in, so we looked up nothing" and
"you are signed in and have nothing here" are different claims — and the anonymous
path never queries the `personal` schema at all.

**Reviews and similar-events are absent from this contract**, not present and empty.
Reviews are ASSUM-6, deferred to Phase 3+. Similar-events needs attendance data that
does not exist — there is no attendance record anywhere in the codebase. An empty
`similar_events: []` would say "we looked and there are none", which is a lie for a
user who *has* attended events the app does not know about.

**"Same area" is city equality, and the deviation is named.** FR-24 defines it as
"haversine distance ≤ 2 km OR same city-zip-cluster", and neither is computable:
`Venue` has no coordinates and there is no zip data. The count is the qualifying
users of *this* event, whose area is the event's own city. FR-24's country rule is
not applied either: the user's home country is not recorded.
EventDetailOut.title: EventDetailOut

EventListOut.description: One page of the public catalog, and what the frontend needs to page through it.
EventListOut.title: EventListOut

EventMuteOut.description:
The outcome of muting or unmuting one event's state-change notices.

**It mirrors `MuteResult` exactly**, because that dataclass already carries the two
facts the client needs and no third: `muted` is the event's *state* after the call,
and `changed` says whether **this call** moved it.

**Muting an already-muted event is a success, not an error** — and `changed: false` is
what says so honestly. A client that redrew on `changed` would redraw a control that
did not move.

**`event_id` is in the response** so the client can confirm which event the answer is
about, without having to trust that the request and the response were about the same
thing.

**This says nothing about the event itself.** A mute silences the correction, not the
event: reminders still fire on the user's Reminder Plan and the event still places in
the Pulse Digest (FR-55). The shape carries no field that could be read as "the event
is off".
EventMuteOut.title: EventMuteOut

EventOut.description:
One public event.

`id` is the stable identifier the API is keyed by; `slug` is the public page route's
key (the spine's Ids convention: a page URL uses the slug, never the PK).
EventOut.title: EventOut

EventPage.description:
The list endpoint's query parameters.

`city` matches the venue's city exactly, case-insensitively. The date bounds are
inclusive and apply to the start time.
EventPage.title: EventPage

EventReportIn.description:
The body of a report: which event, and which of the four things is wrong (FR-59).

**There is no free-text field, and that is a product decision rather than a gap.** FR-57
and FR-59 both put free text in Phase 2. Four fixed categories mean there is nothing for
a user to type into, so there is nothing to moderate, nothing to leak into an editor's
screen, and nothing that needs its own retention rule.
EventReportIn.title: EventReportIn

EventReportOut.description:
What the client needs for the toast, and deliberately nothing else.

**No report id, no tally, no queue state.** A client that could read the tally could
count other people's reports on an event, which is a fact about other users and not
about this one. FR-59 asks only that the user sees "Thanks — we'll review this."

`category` is echoed so an optimistic UI can confirm what it sent without keeping it.
EventReportOut.title: EventReportOut

HealthUnavailableOut.description: The shared error shape, with the per-component details typed for the client.
HealthUnavailableOut.title: HealthUnavailableOut

InterestChipOut.description:
One interest chip: its stable key and its display label.

The **key** is what the API accepts and what is stored; the **label** is what the UI
shows. They are separate because a renamed label must not invalidate a stored pick.
InterestChipOut.title: InterestChipOut

InterestChipsOut.description: The ten interest chips, in the order the flow shows them.
InterestChipsOut.title: InterestChipsOut

InterestsIn.description:
The user's interest picks.

The list **replaces** the user's set: it is the whole set, not a delta. An empty list
is valid — that is how the step is skipped, and it clears the set.

The keys are what is sent, never the labels: a label may be renamed, a key may not.
InterestsIn.title: InterestsIn

MutePromptOut.description:
The "less of this" prompt, when the product should show it.

**The copy is the server's own.** The title names the category the cluster agreed on
and the label comes from `INTEREST_CHIPS` — never from the event's title, which is
untrusted scraped text (AD-9).

**`category_key` is `None` for the generic variant**, when no single chip dominates
the cluster. The client renders the generic copy in that case, and the mute it
creates is a general one rather than a category-specific one.
MutePromptOut.title: MutePromptOut

NoticeDismissOut.description:
The outcome of dismissing one notice.

**`dismissed` and `changed` are two different facts, and the client needs both.**
`dismissed` is the notice's *state* — it is dismissed now. `changed` says whether
**this call** is what made it so.

**The distinction is what makes an idempotent write honest.** Dismissing an
already-dismissed notice is a success, not an error — but a response that claimed
`changed: true` for it would tell the screen to redraw something that did not move.
`changed: false` says "it was already dismissed; nothing changed", which is the truth
and is also what lets the client skip the redraw.

**The same shape as the mute's** (`EventMuteOut`), because both are "a state and
whether this call moved it".
NoticeDismissOut.title: NoticeDismissOut

NoticeListOut.description:
The signed-in user's open notices, newest first.

**A list, and nothing else.** There is no total, no `next` cursor, no page — the strip
shows a few and there is no inbox to page through (FR-54). A `total` would invite the
client to build an inbox, and an inbox is how "one calm correction" becomes a
notification centre.

**`items` is empty, not absent, when the user has no open notices.** An empty list is
the shape; `None` would be a second spelling of the same fact.
NoticeListOut.title: NoticeListOut

NoticeOut.description:
One state-change notice, as the digest strip shows it.

**The notice's own facts, and no more.** The server states what changed and what it
means; the client renders it. The change's *content* — the before/after values — is
deliberately absent: it is source payload, and it is the one place a title or a venue
name could leak into a response (AD-13). `change_kind` is the vocabulary
`domain.lifecycle.ChangeKind` defines, carried through unchanged.

**`event_id` is the catalog event's id, by value.** The client routes to the event's
page, and the notice row holds no relation to the catalog (AD-3).

**`seen_at` and `dismissed_at` are the two different acts.** `seen_at` is when the
notice was put in front of the user — not an act by them. `dismissed_at` is when they
closed it. A notice can be seen and not dismissed, and a client that cannot tell them
apart would render a dismissed notice as still open.

**(Today, a dismissal sets both — but the strip's read deliberately does not mark
notices seen.** A `GET` that writes is the shape CSRF exists to stop, and
`apps/personalization/detail_api.py` refuses it for the Detail Screen. So `seen_at` is
`None` until the user closes the notice. The two stay separate fields because the
moment something *does* mark a notice seen on render, they will say different things.

**`dismissed_at` is `None` on every notice the strip returns**, because the strip is
the queue of *open* notices. It is on the wire anyway so the same shape serves the
Detail banner, which deliberately reports a dismissed notice too.
NoticeOut.title: NoticeOut

NotificationSettingsIn.description:
The settings to save — **only the ones mentioned**.

**Every field is optional, and an omitted field means "leave it alone".** This is a
patch, not a replacement: a client that changes the quiet hours must not clear the
default plan, and a client that only moves the delivery time must not reset the
window.

**`quiet_hours` is the one field where `null` is a value.** An omitted
`quiet_hours` leaves the window alone; a `null` one turns quiet hours **off**. The
two are told apart by the field's *presence in the request*, not by a sentinel, and
the distinction survives because the server reads which fields the client actually
sent.

**The default slots are validated by the same validator the per-event plan uses** — the
same 0-to-4 rule, the same named tiers, the same custom-slot grammar, the same errors.
An empty list is valid and means "new plans start with no reminders".

default_reminder_slots.description: The reminder slots a newly attached plan starts with: 0 to 4 of `5d`, `2d`, `1d`, `1hr`, plus at most one custom slot (`custom:<minutes>`, 15 minutes to 30 days before the event). **Omit this field to leave the default alone**; an empty list means 'no reminders by default'. Changing it does not alter plans that already exist.
default_reminder_slots.title: Default Reminder Slots

digest.description: When and where the daily digest is due. **Omit this field to leave it alone.** The delivery time is a local wall clock and the timezone is the IANA zone it is a clock in; both are required together.

quiet_hours.description: The Quiet Hours window, as two local wall clocks. **Omit this field to leave the window alone; send `null` to turn quiet hours off.** A full-day window (the same clock twice) is refused.

quiet_hours_overrides.description: A quiet-hours window per weekday — **a Pro feature**. Omit this field to leave your per-day windows alone; send `[]` to remove them all and go back to one window for the whole week. The list **replaces** your weekdays rather than merging into them, and the whole week is applied in one transaction. A Free account sending a non-empty list is refused with an upgrade hint.
quiet_hours_overrides.title: Quiet Hours Overrides

NotificationSettingsIn.title: NotificationSettingsIn

NotificationSettingsOut.description:
One user's notification settings — all four facts, in one response.

**One call, one response.** The window and the default slots live on `delivery`'s
`NotificationPreference`; the delivery time and the zone live on `personalization`'s
`DigestPreference`. The split is real and the client should never see it.
NotificationSettingsOut.title: NotificationSettingsOut

OnboardingStateOut.description:
The whole onboarding state: the progress, the interests and the digest preference.

The interests and the digest preference are the **stored** values, so a skipped step
shows what the skip wrote (an empty set, the default preference) rather than nothing.
OnboardingStateOut.title: OnboardingStateOut

OnboardingStatusOut.description:
How far through the onboarding the user is.

This is what `GET /api/auth/me` carries. It says **only** whether the onboarding is
finished and which step the user is on — enough for the frontend to choose between the
onboarding flow and the home. It carries no interests and no digest preference: `me`
is about *who* the user is, and a settings blob there would grow without bound.
OnboardingStatusOut.title: OnboardingStatusOut

PasswordResetConfirmIn.description: The reset confirmation: the token from the reset link, and the new password.
PasswordResetConfirmIn.title: PasswordResetConfirmIn

PasswordResetConfirmOut.description:
The reset-confirmation answer.

The password has been changed and the account's other sessions have ended.
PasswordResetConfirmOut.title: PasswordResetConfirmOut

PasswordResetRequestIn.description: The reset request: the address to reset.
PasswordResetRequestIn.title: PasswordResetRequestIn

PasswordResetRequestOut.description:
The reset-request answer. The same for a known address and an unknown one.

It says the request was received, and nothing about whether there is an account.
PasswordResetRequestOut.title: PasswordResetRequestOut

PersonalEventCreateIn.description:
The body of a create.

The IANA timezone is **required**: a floating local time is refused rather than guessed,
because the user's wall clock and the event's zone are not the same thing.
PersonalEventCreateIn.title: PersonalEventCreateIn

PersonalEventListOut.description: The user's own personal events, soonest first.
PersonalEventListOut.title: PersonalEventListOut

PersonalEventListQuery.description:
The query parameters of the list endpoint.

This is a **separate** schema from `PersonalEventListOut`, and it has to be. A
schema-typed argument is a request *body* unless it is wrapped in `Query(...)`; and the
response schema has no bounds on it, so using it as the query model would silently
accept `?starts_after=…` and then ignore it.

The bounds are inclusive and apply to the start time. Both are optional: with neither,
the list is every event the user has.
PersonalEventListQuery.title: PersonalEventListQuery

PersonalEventOut.description:
One personal event.

`version` rises by one on every edit (AD-7's send key uses it, so it may only go up).

`calendar_connection_id` says where the event came from: a connection's id for a row a
calendar imported, `None` for one the user entered. It is the **id** and nothing else
— the secret address never appears in any response shape (AD-18), and this field does
not change that. Onboarding step 1 needs it to show what a calendar just brought in,
and Settings → Sources will need it to say what a connection owns before it is
disconnected.
PersonalEventOut.title: PersonalEventOut

PersonalEventPatchIn.description:
The body of an edit. Every field is optional — an edit changes only what it names.

A field left out is unchanged. There is no way to *clear* `location` or `notes` through
this shape, because `None` and "not mentioned" are the same value here; that is a
deliberate limitation of a first-cut edit endpoint, not an oversight.
PersonalEventPatchIn.title: PersonalEventPatchIn

PortalOut.description:
The portal answer: the URL to send the user to.

Same shape as the checkout answer and for the same reason — the URL is the whole
answer, and nothing about the subscription rides along with it.
PortalOut.title: PortalOut

PreviewCardOut.description: One card in the Pulse Preview.
PreviewCardOut.title: PreviewCardOut

PreviewCitiesOut.description: The supported cities, for the one-tap city picker.
PreviewCitiesOut.title: PreviewCitiesOut

PreviewOut.description:
The preview for a city.

**`city` is always present**, even when `items` is empty: the empty case is a city
the catalog does not cover, and the frontend shows "No preview available in {city}
yet." — it needs the name to say it. It is never another city's name: an
unsupported explicit city returns an empty preview carrying **that** city's name.
PreviewOut.title: PreviewOut

ProfileIn.description:
The profile write: the name to set.

**One field, and the name is the whole of it.** The email is not editable here — it
is the account's key, and changing it is a different operation with different
consequences. The password is not here either; it is changed by the reset flow,
which ends the account's other sessions.
ProfileIn.title: ProfileIn

ProfileOut.description:
The profile after a write.

**It carries the email and the id as well as the name**, so the client can update
what it already knows without a second `me` call after a save — the name is the only
thing that changed, but the answer is the caller's whole profile rather than a delta.
ProfileOut.title: ProfileOut

PublicEventPageOut.description:
One public event's page facts.

**A separate shape from `EventOut`, deliberately.** `EventOut` is built by
`cls(**vars(event))` over `PublicEvent`, so widening it would change the *catalog
listing's* contract as well — and the listing's contract is not the public page's to
change. The same reasoning that gave the Detail Screen its own shape applies here.

**The fields are the JSON-LD's inputs (AD-12).** ARCHITECTURE-SPINE.md:166 requires
the Schema.org `Event` JSON-LD to be *"emitted from the same data the page renders"*.
So the page's payload carries the title, the description, both times, the zone, the
venue's name and address parts, the canonical URL, the status, the sold-out flag and
the version — one read, everything the page needs.

**`schema_org` is the finished structured data**, projected from the fields above by
`domain.schema_org` and carried on the DTO. The page embeds it verbatim: it does not
build a second object, so it cannot disagree with the one it renders.

**`event_version` is here because the revalidation work item needs it** to prove a
cached page is current.
PublicEventPageOut.title: PublicEventPageOut

QuietHoursIn.description:
A Quiet Hours window to save — two local wall clocks.

**A full-day window is refused.** `start == end` means "quiet all day", which is not a
window but the absence of one, and it is the same statement spelled differently from
"no quiet hours" — so it is refused rather than stored, and "off" has exactly one
spelling on the wire (`null`).

end.description: When quiet hours end, as a local wall clock.
end.title: End

start.description: When quiet hours begin, as a local wall clock.
start.title: Start

QuietHoursIn.title: QuietHoursIn

QuietHoursOut.description:
The Quiet Hours window — two local wall clocks.

`start` and `end` are **wall clocks in the user's own zone**, not instants. A window
that crosses midnight is the normal case, not a special one: `22:00` to `08:00` means
the night, and the server does the arithmetic.

The window is `null` on the wire when the user has turned quiet hours **off** — and
only then. "Never configured" is not a state the window can hold, because reading the
preference creates it with the defaults.
QuietHoursOut.title: QuietHoursOut

QuietHoursOverrideIn.description:
One weekday's quiet-hours window to save (FR-51).

`weekday` is Monday 0 through Sunday 6. A full-day window (`start == end`) is refused
here exactly as it is for the base window, and **the whole list is validated before any
of it is written**, so a bad seventh window does not leave six applied.

end.description: When quiet hours end, as a local wall clock.
end.title: End

start.description: When quiet hours begin that day, as a local wall clock.
start.title: Start

QuietHoursOverrideIn.title: QuietHoursOverrideIn

QuietHoursOverrideOut.description:
One weekday's quiet-hours window, as stored (FR-51).

`weekday` is **Monday 0 through Sunday 6** — `date.weekday()`, the same numbering the
domain and the table use, because a second numbering is a conversion waiting to be got
wrong.

**These are the windows the user stored, not necessarily the ones in force.** A lapsed
Pro account still has its seven here, because they are the user's own data and are never
deleted. What is actually applied is `effective_quiet_hours`.
QuietHoursOverrideOut.title: QuietHoursOverrideOut

ReminderPlanIn.description:
The plan to save.

**0 to 4 slots**, and at most one custom slot. **Zero is a valid save** — FR-9: *"0
slots = no reminders (still in feed)"* — and it is not a delete: the plan row
survives, so "the user chose no reminders" stays distinguishable from "the user never
configured a plan".

**A custom slot's id carries its offset**: `custom:90` is 90 minutes before the
event. The bound is the product's — **15 minutes to 30 days** before the event, from
EXPERIENCE.md — and an out-of-range offset is refused rather than snapped here; the
client snaps it back, and the server refuses it either way.

slots.description: The reminder slots to save: 0 to 4 of `5d`, `2d`, `1d`, `1hr`, plus at most one custom slot. A custom slot is `custom:<minutes>`, where `<minutes>` is an integer from 15 (fifteen minutes before the event) to 43200 (thirty days before the event). An empty list is valid and means 'no reminders'.
slots.title: Slots

ReminderPlanIn.title: ReminderPlanIn

ReminderPlanOut.description:
One event's Reminder Plan, with each slot's computed delivery time.

`slots` is the stored list in the stored order, and `deliveries` carries one entry
per slot in the same order — the picker renders them together, so the two lists
cannot disagree.
ReminderPlanOut.title: ReminderPlanOut

ReminderSlotDeliveryOut.description:
One slot, and when its reminder will actually go out.

`delivery_at` is the **post-Quiet-Hours** instant: the true send time, the same one
stored in the send's `due_at`. A slot whose moment has already passed still carries
its instant — the picker shows what the plan says, and the client decides whether a
past instant is worth rendering differently.

`deferred` says whether Quiet Hours moved it. `deferred_to` is the **window's end**
when it did, and `None` when it did not — the tooltip reads *"Will deliver at {end of
quiet hours}"*, so the client needs that instant and nothing else.

`delivery_at` is `None` only for a slot with no computable offset, which the plan's
own validator refuses on write; it is defensive, not expected.
ReminderSlotDeliveryOut.title: ReminderSlotDeliveryOut

SaveCapDetails.description:
The `details` of a save-cap refusal: the cap, and one upgrade sentence.

**Exactly two fields, and nothing else.** No `modal`, no `title`, no `actions`, no
`dismissable` — the refusal is an *inline* prompt with a quiet "Upgrade" link, not a
modal (EXPERIENCE.md §3, the Free-tier cap prompt). A cap that interrupts with a modal
is a cap that trains people to dismiss prompts. The schema makes the modal-shaped
field inexpressible rather than merely absent from the prose.

This is the same shape `CalendarProviderCapReached` carries (`calendar_connections.py`),
so the two tier caps speak one language to the frontend.
SaveCapDetails.title: SaveCapDetails

SaveCapOut.description:
The 409 a refused save answers with (FR-49).

**A conflict, not a rate limit.** The request was well-formed and the event is
perfectly saveable; the *state of the account* refuses it, because the account has
already spent its allowance. The remedy is not to wait — it is to upgrade — so this is
a 409 and not a 429.

**`code` is a literal, not a bare string**, so this shape can sit in a discriminated
union with the scheduling conflict the same endpoint can answer. See `SaveConflictOut`.
SaveCapOut.title: SaveCapOut

SavedEventListOut.description:
The user's saved events, and how many were left out.

`omitted` counts the saves whose catalog event has since disappeared — superseded or
unpublished. They are not listed, because they have no title to show, but they are not
hidden either: the count lets the client tell the user that something they saved is no
longer available, rather than silently dropping it.
SavedEventListOut.title: SavedEventListOut

SavedEventListQuery.description:
The query parameters of the saved-events list endpoint.

The bounds are inclusive and apply to the **snapshot's** start time — the same value the
list returns — so a filtered item and its own timestamp never disagree (AD-21).
SavedEventListQuery.title: SavedEventListQuery

SavedEventOut.description:
One saved public event.

**The times come from the snapshot; the display fields come from the catalog.** They
are two different places, and keeping them straight is the point (AD-21):

- `start_time_utc` and `end_time_utc` are the **snapshot** — what the user saw when
  they saved, updated only by AD-17 propagation.
- `title`, `venue_name` and `canonical_url` are the **catalog's current** values, read
  at request time. An editorial correction shows up immediately.

`event_version` is the snapshot's version of the catalog event. It is what lets the
system detect that the snapshot is behind, and it is what `stale` is measured against.
SavedEventOut.title: SavedEventOut

SchedulingConflictDetails.description: The `details` of a 409: which event was written, and what it clashes with.
SchedulingConflictDetails.title: SchedulingConflictDetails

SchedulingConflictOut.description:
The 409 a conflicting create or edit answers with.

It is an `ErrorOut` — `{code, message, details?}` — with the `details` field
**narrowed** to the conflict payload. That narrowing is the point: the client has to
render the three actions (FR-58), so the shape of the conflict has to be in the
generated contract, not just in the prose of the description. With the plain `ErrorOut`
the `details` would be an untyped dictionary, and a client generated from the OpenAPI
document could not read a single field of it.

The message and code come from `domain.errors.SchedulingConflictError`; the API layer
builds the body, so the two stay in step through this schema.

**`code` is a literal, not a bare string**, so this shape can sit in a discriminated
union with the save-cap refusal the same endpoint can answer. See `SaveConflictOut`.
SchedulingConflictOut.title: SchedulingConflictOut

SignInIn.description: The sign-in request: an address and a password.
SignInIn.title: SignInIn

SignInOut.description:
The sign-in answer. The same for a wrong password and an unknown address.

The status is the only field. A body that named the account, or said which half of
the pair was wrong, would be the enumeration leak the services are careful to avoid.
SignInOut.title: SignInOut

SignOutOut.description: The sign-out answer. The session is over; nothing else is said.
SignOutOut.title: SignOutOut

SignUpIn.description:
The sign-up request: an address, a password, and optionally a home city.

The password is a plain string here and is never echoed back. It goes to
`apps.identity.services.sign_up`, which validates it against Django's configured
password validators and hashes it.

**`city` is optional, and it is the visitor's preview choice carried across
sign-up.** The preview choice lives in a **session cookie** read in the browser
only — deliberately, because a server-side choice would make `/preview` vary per
visitor and break AD-12's cacheability. So the carry is a **request field**: the
frontend reads the cookie and sends the city here.

A city the catalog does not cover is stored as the fallback with `city_source`
`fallback`, so the digest can say "we don't have your city yet" rather than passing
the fallback off as the user's city. The sign-up **response** says nothing about
it either way — a city is not an account-existence oracle, but the response shape
carries nothing beyond `status` in any case.
SignUpIn.title: SignUpIn

SignUpOut.description:
The sign-up answer. The same for a new address and an existing one.

There is no `created` flag, and no account id: either would say whether the address
was taken. The account holder of an existing address is told by email instead.
SignUpOut.title: SignUpOut

SourceGroupOut.description:
One group of sources — Official, Community, Aggregator or Crawled.

**The four groups are always present, even when empty.** The screen renders a heading
per group, and a group that appeared and disappeared as the registry changed would
make the screen's shape depend on the data.
SourceGroupOut.title: SourceGroupOut

SourceListOut.description:
Every source in the registry, grouped.

**`groups` is the whole registry**, in the order the screen shows it. A registry with
no sources answers with four empty groups rather than an error — an empty registry is
an answer, and the screen has a quiet empty state for it.
SourceListOut.title: SourceListOut

SourceMuteResultOut.description:
The outcome of setting one source's mute state.

**`changed` says whether the call did anything.** Setting the state a source was
already in is a success, not an error — but a response claiming a change when none
happened would make the screen redraw something that did not move.
SourceMuteResultOut.title: SourceMuteResultOut

SourceMuteSetIn.description: The request body for setting one source's mute state.
SourceMuteSetIn.title: SourceMuteSetIn

SourceOut.description:
One source in the registry, as the screen shows it.

**`id` is the catalog Source's id, by value.** The mute is keyed on it, and the
client sends it back on the write — so the id the screen shows and the id the mute
uses are the same one.

**`mute_state` is this user's state for this source**, and it is `"default"` for a
source the user has never touched. It is not `None`: the control has three
positions, and "no preference" is one of them.
SourceOut.title: SourceOut

SourceRestoreDefaultsOut.description:
The outcome of the bulk reset.

**`removed` is how many preferences were cleared**, so the screen can say what
happened rather than just that it happened.
SourceRestoreDefaultsOut.title: SourceRestoreDefaultsOut

SourceTrustOut.description:
One source's trust, as the screen renders it.

**`band` is the 1–5 count the dots draw**, and it is the server's number. The client
draws `band` filled dots and `5 - band` empty ones; it does not compute the band from
`score`, because the boundaries are the server's rule and a client that recomputed
them would be a second opinion about what a score means.

**`score` is the raw FR-16 posterior**, in [0, 1]. It is here for the client's own
tooltips and for a future "why is this source low?" — not for the dots.

**`band` is never a delta.** A week-over-week drop is provably impossible
(`domain/reliability.py`), so there is no "down" state to render.
SourceTrustOut.title: SourceTrustOut

SubscriptionOut.description:
The caller's entitlement: one bool and nothing else.

**The minimum, on purpose.** This answers exactly one question — *may this person buy
a plan?* — and the answer is a bool. There is no plan name, no renewal date and no
status here, because the fuller subscription record belongs to the account-and-billing
surface, which needs a wider read and builds it there. A field here would be a field
two callers could disagree about.

**It is a read of the caller's own entitlement.** There is no user id in the request
and none in the response: the user comes from the session, so a caller cannot ask
about somebody else.
SubscriptionOut.title: SubscriptionOut

TimelineBlockOut.description:
One block on one day of the Timeline.

**`id` is the id the screen acts on.** For a personal block it is the personal event's
id; for a public block it is the **catalog** event's id, so the screen routes to
`/events/:id` without knowing which table it came from.

**`name` is nullable, and that is a state rather than a hole.** A save whose catalog
event has disappeared has no title to show — the save is still the user's own record
and its snapshot still has a time, so the block is still drawn, and the client says
"event no longer available" rather than showing a blank.

**`start_time_tz` is the event's own zone**, not the zone the week is cut in. A public
event in Berlin, shown to a user in Los Angeles, is on a different Los Angeles day than
its own clock suggests — so the block carries its own zone, and the response carries
the user's zone separately.

**`conflict` is already decided.** The server projects the pairs onto the blocks, so
the screen does not have to know what a conflict pair is, and the two surfaces — the
Pulse Card and the Timeline — cannot disagree about which block is flagged.

**`state` is the catalog's lifecycle word**, carried through unchanged — the same
`str` the event detail and the public page already carry, because the vocabulary is
the backend's and a second one here would be a translation layer with nothing to
translate. It is null for a personal block, which has no lifecycle, and for a public
block whose catalog event has disappeared, where the state is unknown rather than
normal — the same distinction `name` already draws.

A `cancelled` block is still returned. FR-55 removes a cancelled event from the
*digest*; the Timeline is the user's calendar, and a cancelled event is still on it
until they take it off.
TimelineBlockOut.title: TimelineBlockOut

TimelineDayOut.description:
One local day, with its blocks in time order.

**A multi-day event appears on every day it covers.** An event running from Friday
22:00 to Saturday 02:00 is a Friday block *and* a Saturday block, and the indicator
fires on whichever day-cell the overlap falls in.
TimelineDayOut.title: TimelineDayOut

TimelineOut.description:
One Mon–Sun week, in the user's timezone.

**Seven days, always.** An empty week still has seven day cells, each with an empty
`blocks` list — the screen draws seven columns, and it should not have to know whether
the week has anything in it.

`timezone` is the zone the days were cut in, so the client can label the week without
guessing.
TimelineOut.title: TimelineOut

TimelineQuery.description:
The query parameters of the Timeline endpoint.

**`week` is any date in the wanted week.** The response names that week's Monday and
Sunday, so the client does not have to know which day of the week it asked for. With
no `week`, the current week in the user's own zone is returned — the user's zone, not
the server's, because a week is cut at local midnight.

A malformed value is a 422: the parameter is typed as a date, so Django Ninja's own
validation answers it, on the same path every other malformed query in this codebase
takes.
TimelineQuery.title: TimelineQuery

UrlFeedEntryOut.description:
One publicly addressable URL, and when it last changed.

**`path` is a path, not a URL.** The origin is the frontend's business — the sitemap
resolves each path against the site's own public origin — so the backend hands over
a path and never an absolute URL. That keeps the backend free of any knowledge of
how the frontend is deployed, and it keeps one origin in one place.

**`kind` is a closed vocabulary.** `event` and `city` are the two kinds of public
page the site serves, and a third kind would have to be declared here too — a kind
that exists on only one side of the wire is a kind nobody can serve.

**`last_modified` is the page's real last change.** It is derived from the event's
state history, not from a timestamp of convenience, so a crawler is told the truth
about what moved.
UrlFeedEntryOut.title: UrlFeedEntryOut

UrlFeedOut.description:
One page of the public URL feed, and what the caller needs to page through it.

**`total` is the size of the whole feed**, so a caller can decide how many children
its sitemap index needs before it fetches the first child — and that is exactly what
the sitemap's index route does.

**`has_next` is measured against `total`**, so a caller knows when to stop without
fetching a page that would be empty.
UrlFeedOut.title: UrlFeedOut

UrlFeedQuery.description:
The URL feed endpoint's query parameters.

**Bounded at the edge, and the edge is a refusal** — the same rule the city page's
query follows, for the same reason: this read grows with the catalog, and a caller
that asks for a million URLs at once has made a mistake. The service below the
surface clamps rather than refuses, because it is also called directly by code that
is not an HTTP request.
UrlFeedQuery.title: UrlFeedQuery

WebhookAck.description:
What the provider gets back. A slug naming the outcome, and nothing else.

No subscription id, no user id, no plan: a webhook response is read by a provider and by
whoever can replay a delivery, and it has no reason to carry anything about the account.
WebhookAck.title: WebhookAck

WhyThisOut.description:
The persisted why-this breakdown (FR-24, AD-10).

**This is a persisted fact, not a computation.** The tags, the bucket and the badge
are the `DigestComposition` row's own values, read back from the most recent
composition for that `(user, event)` pair. AD-10 says an explanation "is never
generated at view time", and this is where that either holds or is quietly broken.

**The bucket, not the score.** FR-22's raw `relevance_score` is an internal number;
the screen shows 1–5 dots. Sending the score would invite the frontend to re-bucket
it — the "recomputed at render" failure wearing a different hat.

**The tags are the persisted keys, in the persisted order.** The client owns the
labels; the server states the facts.

**The Source Badge is the variant key, or `None`.** A personal event has no source,
so it has no badge; `None` here means "there is no source", not "unknown".
WhyThisOut.title: WhyThisOut

get.description: The CSRF token the frontend sends back on every state-changing request, in the `X-CSRFToken` header. The token is also set as the `csrftoken` cookie on this response, so the frontend can read it from there. This is a safe request, so it is not itself checked for a token.
get.summary: Get a CSRF token

get.description: The signed-in user's id, email, name and onboarding status. An anonymous request is refused with 401. Nothing internal is returned: there is no password hash, no permission list and no catch-all field. The name is empty when no name is set; the frontend renders its own fallback in that case. The onboarding status says only whether the onboarding is finished and which step the user is on; the full state is at `/api/personal/onboarding`.
get.summary: The signed-in user

post.description: Asks for a reset link. A known address gets one, by transactional email; an unknown address gets nothing. The answer is the same either way, so the endpoint cannot be used to find out who has an account.

Consumes a reset token and sets a new password. The token is single-use and short-lived: a token that was already used, revoked or expired is refused, and the refusal does not say which of the three it was. The account's other sessions end, so a stolen session does not survive the password change.

put.description:
Sets the name the product addresses this account by. An empty name is legal and means "no name set" — the frontend falls back to a name derived from the email address in that case. A name carrying a line break or a control character is refused with 422 and nothing is written.

This is a `PUT`, not a `PATCH`: it is the one verb this product's settings writes use, and a second verb for the same write would put two shapes for one operation into the contract.

post.description: Authenticates an email and a password and establishes the session. A wrong password and an unknown address are answered identically — the same status and the same body — so neither can be used to find out who has an account.
Ends the session the request carries. The session cookie is cleared, so the next request is anonymous.

Creates an account. The answer is the same whether the address was new or already taken: an existing account holder is told by email instead. This endpoint does not sign anyone in — call `/api/auth/signin` for that — so the response is byte-identical and header-identical whichever case it was.

`city` is optional: the visitor's home city, carried across from the preview choice. A city the catalog does not cover is stored as the fallback, and the response says nothing about it either way.

get.description:
Reads the signed-in user's plan state: status, plan, when the current term ends, and whether a payment needs fixing.

**This is the wider read `/subscription` deliberately is not.** That endpoint answers one bit — may this person use Pro — and stays one bit on purpose. This one carries what a person needs in order to act on their own subscription.

**`is_pro` is true for `past_due`, and `needs_payment` is how they differ.** A failed payment leaves someone entitled while they fix it, so a screen reading only the bool would show a person with a recoverable problem exactly what it shows a person with none.

**`period_end` is not a renewal date.** This product does not model `cancel_at_period_end`, so a subscription cancelled in the provider's portal reads `active` until its term runs out. The field says when the term ends, which is true whether or not it will renew.

**The user comes from the session**, so a caller cannot ask about somebody else. Read-only: no provider call, no session minted, nothing written.
get.summary: Read the caller's plan for the account screen

post.description:
Mints a checkout session for the chosen plan and returns the URL to send the user to.

**The body carries the plan and nothing else.** The success and cancel URLs are built from this deployment's configuration, so a client cannot name them.

**Paying does not make you Pro yet.** The provider's webhook is what records the subscription; this endpoint writes nothing. If the webhook has not landed, the user is still on the free tier — which is why the response carries no entitlement field.

**A user who already has a live subscription is refused** with 409, and the response points at the portal: that is where an existing subscription is managed. Starting a second checkout would create a second subscription to notice and cancel.

Opens the provider's customer portal for the signed-in user, where they manage their plan, their card and their cancellation, and returns the URL to send them to.

**The provider is called with the stored customer reference.** No reference is taken from the request, so a caller cannot open another account's portal by naming one.

**A user with no subscription is refused** with 409 — there is no customer to open a portal against, and the answer says so plainly rather than letting the provider explain a customer that does not exist.

get.description:
Reads whether the signed-in user is entitled to Pro, and returns a single boolean.

**This is the only read on the billing surface.** The other two endpoints are actions — they mint a checkout session and they mint a portal session — so neither can answer 'may this person buy a plan?' without a side effect. This one is read-only: no provider is called, no session is minted and nothing is written.

**The user comes from the session.** There is no id in the request and none in the response, so a caller cannot ask about somebody else's subscription.

**It carries a bool and nothing else.** No plan, no renewal date, no status: the answer to this question is one bit, and the fuller record belongs to the account-and-billing surface.

**`past_due` reads as Pro.** A payment that failed leaves the person entitled while they fix it, and the portal is where they fix it.
get.summary: Read the caller's entitlement

get.description: One city page — the read behind `/events-in-{city}` (FR-27). A paged listing of the city's upcoming public events, best Event Fit first, each with the persisted fit's score and tags. A city below the publishing threshold comes back with `is_published=false` and no events, which the page renders as 'coming soon' — it does not 404, because a URL that vanishes after ranking throws away every bit of ranking it earned. An unknown slug is a 404. No session is used and none is set.
get.summary: Get one city page, by slug

get.description: Published, non-superseded events that have not started yet, soonest first. Optional city and date-range filters. No session is used and none is set.
get.summary: List upcoming public events

get.description: One published event by slug — the read behind `/events/{slug}` (FR-26). Unlike the listing's read, an event that has already happened still resolves: the page stays addressable and stays indexed. An event that is not public reads as not found. No session is used and none is set.
get.summary: Get one public event page, by slug

get.description: One published event by id. An event that is not public — or that has already started — reads as not found, the same set the list shows. No session is used and none is set.
get.summary: Get one public event

get.description: One page of the public URL feed: every publicly addressable page — a public event's page and a qualifying city's page — with the time each last really changed. This is the sitemap's source, so it lists exactly the URLs the site serves: no unpublished event, no superseded event, and no city below the publishing threshold. The read is paged and bounded, because it grows with the catalog. No session is used and none is set.
get.summary: List the site's publicly addressable URLs

get.description: Redirects to the link's destination. **A redirect, not an open pixel**: SM-2 measures the digest CTA click and rejects open-pixel measurement as unreliable. The click passes through our server, so it is trackable. The destination is inside the signed token, and it must be one of ours, so the link cannot be edited into an open redirect.
get.summary: Follow a tracked link

get.description: Renders a confirmation page for an unsubscribe link. **Nothing changes.** A `GET` must never unsubscribe anyone: mail clients and security scanners follow links in a message automatically, and a `GET` that unsubscribed would let a mail provider cancel a subscription the user never touched. The page says what would be turned off and offers the inverse.
get.summary: What an unsubscribe link would turn off

post.description:
Applies the unsubscribe the signed token names. **This is the RFC 8058 one-click path**, and it is deliberately unauthenticated: the provider that makes the request has no session, so the signed token is the authorisation. The token names the user, the scope and the target, and cannot be forged or edited.

Two scopes, and they never touch each other: an event scope turns off that event's reminders and leaves the daily digest alone; the Pulse Ping scope turns off the digest and leaves every reminder plan alone. Applying a scope also cancels that scope's pending sends, so the mail the user just turned off is not delivered afterwards.

get.description: The Detail Screen's data. A signed-in caller also receives their own why-this breakdown, their saved state, the k-anonymous neighbor count, and their active conflict pair for this event if there is one; an anonymous caller receives the public facts and nothing personal. An event that is not public — or that has already started — reads as not found, the same set the public catalog shows.
get.summary: Get one event's Detail Screen

post.description: Records that the signed-in user opened this event's Detail Screen, which is one of the two signals that make a user count as a neighbor (FR-24). The signal is recorded once per `(user, event)`: opening the screen again refreshes the timestamp rather than adding a row. Anonymous callers are refused.
post.summary: Record that the Detail Screen was opened

post.description:
Starts building a JSON and an ICS export of this account's data. The links arrive by email within 24 hours.

**Available to every signed-in account**, on any tier: data portability is a right under GDPR Article 20, not a paid feature.

**Asking twice while one is already building returns the request in flight** rather than starting a second one, so a double-click costs nothing.
post.summary: Request an export of everything we hold about you

get.description: How far along one of this user's exports is.
get.summary: Check on one of your export requests

get.description:
Returns the export file itself. **Authenticated by the signed token in the link, not by a session** — the link is followed from a mail client, which has none.

The token names the export, the account and the format together, so none of the three can be changed in the URL. A link is refused once the export expires, whatever its signature says.
get.summary: Download an export with its emailed link
Health

get.description:
The notices the user has not dismissed, newest first — the data behind the digest home's strip.

**A few, not a history.** The list is bounded by the server: FR-54 promises one calm correction, not a notification centre, and there is no inbox to page through. An empty list is the common case — most users, most days, have nothing to correct.

**A notice is here until it is dismissed.** Being shown a notice is not the same as acting on it, so the strip is a queue: it empties when the user closes an item, not when it renders.

**This says nothing about the event.** A notice names the change and the event it is about; it does not say the event is cancelled, moved, or off. The client renders the correction; the event's own page carries its facts.
get.summary: The signed-in user's open state-change notices

delete.description:
Clears the mute on one event, so its "this changed" messages come back.

**Unmuting does not replay what was silenced.** The notices suppressed while the mute was on are gone, and raising them now would deliver a correction about a change the user has had days to notice. The event's current state is on its Detail screen, which is where a user who just unmuted is standing.

**Unmuting an event that is not muted is a success**, and the response says `changed: false`.
delete.summary: Let one event's state-change notices through again

put.description:
Mutes FR-54's notices for one event: the "this changed" message stops.
