**A mute silences the correction, not the event.** Reminders still fire on the user's Reminder Plan and the event still places in the Pulse Digest. There is no global off switch — a per-event mute is a judgement about the one event the user is looking at.

**A cancellation is still raised.** A cancelled or superseded event is announced even when muted, because the mute has already removed it from the digest and silence about it would have no second channel to catch it.

**Muting an already-muted event is a success**, and the response says `changed: false` — nothing moved.

**No existence check on the event.** A mute for an event that has since gone is harmless, and refusing it would make the mute fail in exactly the case a user most wants it.
put.summary: Silence the state-change notices for one event

post.description:
Closes one notice: it leaves the strip, and it never comes back. This is a real write, not client state — dismissal is what makes FR-54's "one-time, never repeats" true.

**The notice row survives.** It is closed, not deleted, so the daily cap and the never-repeat rule still hold against it.

**Dismissing an already-dismissed notice is a success**, and the response says `changed: false` — nothing moved, and the client need not redraw.

**A notice that is not yours, or that does not exist, is a 404** — the same 404 for both, so the endpoint cannot be used to find out whether a given id exists.

get.description:
The signed-in user's Browse surface: public events in their city across a seven-day window, ranked by the same Relevance Pulse the Pulse Digest uses, with the save state of each card.

The city is the user's **digest preference** city, not a parameter — one meaning of 'your city' across both surfaces, which is why the surface's 'Change city' link goes to account settings. A user who skipped onboarding has no city: the response says `city_missing` and carries no cards, and the client shows the same quiet empty state it shows for a city with nothing on.

The window is cut in the **user's** timezone, so an event at 11pm local on the seventh day is inside it and one at 1am the next morning is not.

`total` is how many events the user can page to, and `tier_2_starts_at` is where the second section begins — the server names the tiers so the rule cannot drift from the Digest's. `quota` reports the save allowance **without spending it**: it is a sign above the gate, not the gate.

Each card carries up to three Why-this Tag keys, the Confidence Pulse bucket and the Source Badge variant, plus `is_saved` so an already-saved event renders as saved on first paint. At most one card per response carries the `must_know` stripe.
get.summary: Browse the user's city, tonight and the next seven days

get.description: The user's own calendar connections: the provider, the status, when it last synced and whether a sync is running. The calendar address is **never** returned — it is the credential, and it is write-only. No one else's connections are listed.
get.summary: List the signed-in user's calendar connections

post.description:
Connects a calendar by its secret ICS/webcal address. The address is stored encrypted and is never returned. The first sync is **enqueued, not run inline** — the response comes back immediately with the connection's status, and the import lands a moment later. A Free account may hold one calendar; a second connection is refused with a calm upgrade prompt.

**The cap is chosen by tier (FR-50): one for Free, three for Pro.** A Pro account may connect a second and a third; a fourth is refused. The refusal is a 409 carrying `cap` and one calm `upgrade_hint` — an inline prompt, not a modal. A Pro account that lapses keeps the connections it already has: the cap is enforced when connecting, not by deleting what the user already owns.

delete.description: Disconnects one of the user's calendars. The credential is destroyed and the events that calendar imported are purged, along with their conflict pairs and their reminder plans. The user's own events are untouched.

get.description: One of the user's own calendar connections and its sync state, so onboarding step 1 can show the imported events without leaving the flow. A connection that belongs to somebody else reads as not found.
get.summary: Get one of the signed-in user's calendar connections

post.description: Replaces a revoked calendar's address and brings it back to life. The events it already imported are kept — the provider revoked the address, not the events. A connection that is already active is refused: there is nothing to reconnect, and silently replacing a working credential would change which calendar the user is looking at without them asking.
post.summary: Reconnect a calendar whose access was revoked

get.description:
This user's collections in the order they arranged, each with how many saves it holds.

**Open on every tier.** A lapsed Pro user's collections do not vanish — the brief forbids deleting a downgraded account's data, and a list that hid them would be that deletion as far as the user could tell.
get.summary: List your collections

post.description:
Creates an empty collection at the end of this user's list.

**Pro only.** A Free account is refused with 409 and a `{cap, upgrade_hint}` payload — the same inline-prompt shape the save cap and the calendar cap use, with no modal-shaped field.

**It is created empty**, which is an ordinary state rather than a half-finished one: membership is explicit, so nothing is ever filed into a collection the user did not put it in.

**The name is unique per user, case-insensitively** — 'Weekend' and 'weekend' are one name — and is stored exactly as typed.

put.description:
Takes the **whole ordering in one request**, so the server never observes a partially reordered list.

**The complete list, never a move instruction.** 'Put this one third' has to be interpreted against a list that may have changed since the client read it; a complete order is unambiguous. A list that does not name every collection exactly once is refused, because the unnamed ones would otherwise land somewhere nobody asked for.

**Open on every tier.**
put.summary: Set the order of your collections

delete.description:
Deletes a collection and **leaves every save inside it untouched** — they simply become uncollected.

**Open on every tier.** This is the one delete the intent permits, and what it deletes is a grouping rather than user content. Gating it would trap a lapsed user with data they want gone, which is the inverse of what the never-delete constraint is for.

The remaining collections close up, so positions stay dense.

patch.description:
Renames one of this user's collections.

**Open on every tier.** Gating a rename would mean a lapsed user cannot fix a typo in a name they wrote themselves, which is punishment for lapsing rather than a tier boundary.

**Renaming to the name it already has is allowed** and is not a collision with itself. Another collection's name is refused with 409.

get.description:
The saves in one collection, newest addition first.

**The snapshot, and only the snapshot.** The times come from the user's own `SavedEvent` rows, which AD-17 propagation keeps correct — there is no `catalog` read here, because AD-3 forbids relating the two schemas and the snapshot is what the Timeline and the conflict detector already use.

A surface that wants titles and venues uses `GET /api/personal/saved-events`, which is the endpoint that owns that join.
get.summary: List the saves in a collection

delete.description:
Removes a membership. **The save itself is untouched** — it simply stops being in this collection.

**Open on every tier**, and deliberately so: this is how a lapsed Pro user tidies up, and refusing it would trap them with an arrangement they cannot change.

Removing something that is not there is a no-op.
delete.summary: Take a save out of a collection

put.description:
Assigns one of this user's saves to one of their collections.

**Pro only**, and refused with the same `{cap, upgrade_hint}` payload as a create. Without this gate the cap would limit how many collections exist and not how much they are used.

**Idempotent**: a save already in the collection is the same statement twice, so it answers 204 and writes no audit row.

**A save can be in several collections at once** — membership is a table, not a column.
put.summary: Put a save into a collection

get.description:
Every conflict pair the signed-in user has, in two groups: `active` — what still needs a decision — and `resolved` — what was decided. Each pair carries both sides, named, so a pair can be shown without a second request per side.

**A saved side is named by its catalog title.** A save has no title of its own; the title lives in the catalog and is read through its published interface. A side whose record is gone reads as `available: false` with no name — 'event no longer available' — rather than a blank or an error.

**`resolved` holds the pairs the user answered.** A pair closed because a side went away without the user answering (`cleared_by_state_change`) is not listed: it is not the user's choice, so it is not presented as one.

Active pairs are ordered by the earlier side's start time, soonest first; resolved pairs by resolution time, newest first. No other user's pairs are readable.
get.summary: List the signed-in user's conflict pairs

get.description:
The user's Pulse Digest for their local day, as it was composed.

The response always says which state it is in: `composed` (there is a digest and it has cards), `empty` (there is a digest and it has none — nothing qualifying near you today), or `not_composed` (the digest has not been built yet). The last two are different facts and the client shows different things for them.

Each card carries the event's name, time and place, up to three Why-this Tag keys, the Confidence Pulse bucket (1-5) and the Source Badge variant. The bucket is sent rather than the raw score: the bucket the user saw this morning is a persisted fact about their day, and a client that re-bucketed it could flicker.

The times are instants plus an IANA timezone; converting them for display is the client's job. `catalog_event_missing` marks a card whose event the catalog no longer holds — the explanation is still there, because a composition is a fact about the day.

A card also carries the event's current `status` (`scheduled`, `postponed` or `cancelled`) and whether it `is_sold_out`. These are read at request time, not stored on the composition, so an event that changed after the composition still says so. Both are `null` for a personal event — the user's own agenda row has no lifecycle and no tickets — and `null` for a card whose event the catalog no longer holds.
get.summary: The signed-in user's Pulse Digest for today

post.description:
Records one dismissal and tells the client whether the product should now ask the "less of this" question.

**The slot is read, not sent.** The service resolves it from the user's own composition, so a client cannot claim a dismissal came from a slot it did not come from — and cannot put a serendipity card into the cluster by asserting it did.

**`prompt_due` is the whole answer.** It is true when three similar events have been dismissed in a digest window, and it stays true for that one call — the cluster's counter resets when the prompt fires, so the same cluster cannot nag.

**A dismissal that did not advance the cluster was still recorded.** The user really did dismiss it; the product just does not count it.
post.summary: Record that the user swiped past an event

post.description:
Records one report against a public event (FR-59). The body names the event and exactly one of four categories; there is no free-text field.

**A report never changes what anyone can see.** The event stays in the digest and on its public page until an editor decides. One person cannot pull a listing.

Five reports per user per day; the sixth answers 429 with the wait. Reporting the same event for the same reason twice is accepted and counted once — the editor's tally counts people, not taps.

An event that does not exist, or that is not publicly visible, answers 404 — the same refusal the event detail read gives, so this endpoint cannot be used to find out whether a hidden event exists.
post.summary: Report a catalog event as wrong

get.description: The user's own personal events, soonest first. No one else's are listed.
get.summary: List the signed-in user's personal events

post.description: Creates a personal event. The IANA timezone is required — a floating local time is refused rather than guessed. If the new event clashes with one already on the calendar, the response is 409 carrying the conflict and the three actions; the client then posts one of them to the resolve endpoint.

Records the user's choice on a conflict prompt. Exactly one of the three actions the prompt offered is accepted; there is no dismiss. A resolution that is illegal for this conflict's kind — or for the side named — is refused, and the prompt stays open.

**The request names the side the action is about**, with its kind, because the pair row is symmetric and cannot say which side the user is acting on. The action decides what it may act on: `delete_new` deletes a personal event and refuses a saved side; `skip_public` releases a save of a public event and refuses a personal side. So a client cannot delete a personal event by naming a saved side, and it cannot release another user's save by naming a personal one — a side that is not one of the pair's two is refused outright.

delete.description: Removes one of the signed-in user's personal events.

get.description: One of the signed-in user's personal events. An event that is not theirs reads as not found.
get.summary: Get one personal event

patch.description: Edits a personal event and re-runs conflict detection. A conflicting edit returns the same 409 payload a conflicting create does.

get.description: Where the user is in the 3-step onboarding flow, their interest picks and their digest delivery preference. A user who left mid-step is resumed at the same step within 7 days; after that the flow restarts at step 1. A user who has finished onboarding is never sent back into it.
get.summary: The signed-in user's onboarding state

put.description:
Sets when and where the Pulse Digest should arrive. The delivery time is a local wall clock, so it means nine in the morning where the user is. The timezone must be an IANA zone name.

`city` is the user's home city, in the catalog's own spelling. A city the catalog does not cover is stored as the fallback and reported back with `city_source` set to `fallback`, so the client can say "we don't have your city yet" rather than implying it is the user's city.

`include_personal_events` defaults to included — personal events are in the digest unless the user opts out. Both fields are optional, and **leaving one out does not change it**: an omitted field (and a `null` city) means "leave it alone", so a client that only wants to change the delivery time does not reset the city. This endpoint cannot clear the city — a `null` and an omitted field are the same value, and a shape that cannot tell them apart must not guess.
put.summary: Set the digest delivery time, timezone, home city and personal-events opt-out

get.description: The ten interest chips, in the order the flow shows them. This list comes from the server, so the frontend holds no second copy of it. Each chip carries a stable `key` and a display `label` — send the key back, not the label.
get.summary: The interest chips on offer

put.description: Replaces the user's interest picks with the given set. At most 3 chips may be picked, and every key must be one the chips endpoint offers. An empty list is valid — that is how the step is skipped, and it clears the set.

post.description: Skips every step and finishes the onboarding. A user who skips everything has still finished onboarding — the default digest preference is written, so the digest has a delivery time to work with.
Moves the user to the next step. Advancing past the last step finishes the onboarding — there is no fourth step. A user who has already finished is not moved again.
post.summary: Advance to the next onboarding step

post.description: Skips the current step. No step requires any input, so every one of them can be skipped. Skipping the interests step clears the picks; skipping the digest step writes the default delivery preference. Skipping the last step finishes the onboarding.

get.description: The user's own saved events, soonest first. The times are the snapshots — what the user saw when they saved — and the titles and venues are the catalog's current values. `omitted` counts the saves whose catalog event has since disappeared; they are not listed, but they are not hidden either.
get.summary: List the signed-in user's saved events

delete.description: Removes one of the signed-in user's saves. The conflict pairs it took part in close as `cleared_by_state_change` — the pair ended because a side went away, which is not a user resolution.

post.description:
Saves a public catalog event onto the signed-in user's own calendar. The save is idempotent: saving an event that is already saved returns the existing record. The times in the response are the snapshot taken at save time; `stale` says whether the catalog has moved past it, in which case re-propagation has been requested.

If the save clashes with a personal event, the response is 409 carrying the conflict and the three actions. **The third action is `skip_public`** — because the side the user just added is a *save*, the destructive choice releases the save rather than deleting a record. The conflict names both sides with their kinds, so the client has everything it needs to post the resolution.

**A Free account may save one event per day (FR-49).** A second save inside that window is refused with a 409 carrying `cap` and one calm `upgrade_hint` — an inline prompt, not a modal. A Pro account has no such cap. The two 409s are told apart by `code`: `scheduling_conflict` for a clash, `save_cap_reached` for the cap.

get.description:
One Mon–Sun week in the **user's timezone**, as seven days, each a time-ordered list of blocks — the user's personal events and their saved public events, merged.

**`week` is any date in the wanted week.** The response names that week's Monday and Sunday. With no `week`, the current week in the user's own zone is returned. A malformed value is a 422.

**Days are cut in the user's timezone**, not the server's — a week is cut at local midnight, so it is 167 hours across a spring-forward and 169 across a fall-back. An event is placed on the day its local start falls on.

**A block carries the id the screen acts on**: the personal event's id, or the *catalog* event's id for a saved event, so the screen can route to `/events/:id`. It also carries the event's own zone, which is not the zone the week is cut in.

**`conflict` is already decided.** It is true on both sides of an active pair, and it stays true after 'Keep both' — that resolution leaves a permanent reminder. Every other resolution clears it.

**A multi-day event appears on every day it covers**, and the indicator fires on the day-cell whose interval contains the **overlap** — the clash itself, not the event's whole span. So an event running from Friday 22:00 to Saturday 02:00 that clashes on Friday lights Friday's cell only, while a clash that itself straddles midnight lights both of its days.

**Seven days, always** — an empty week still has seven day cells. No other user's events are readable.
get.summary: The signed-in user's week, day by day

get.description: Up to three Pulse Cards for a city, each with its Event Fit score and Why-this tags and its Source Badge. With no `city` parameter the city is inferred from the edge's geo header; an explicit `city` overrides it; `use_geo=false` is the visitor's 'Don't use my location' choice and the location is then not consulted at all. The response says which city was resolved and how it was resolved. No session is used and none is set.
get.summary: The Pulse Preview for a city

get.description: The supported cities, alphabetically, for the one-tap city picker. A city is supported when the catalog has at least one upcoming public event with an Event Fit for it. No session is used and none is set.
get.summary: The cities the Pulse Preview can serve

get.description:
The signed-in user's Reminder Plan for one event, and for each slot the instant its reminder will **actually** go out.

**The delivery time is the server's answer, not the client's arithmetic.** It is the post-Quiet-Hours instant — already deferred, if the slot would have fallen inside the user's quiet window — so the picker can dim that chip and show *"Will deliver at 8:00 am Saturday"* without reimplementing the shift (where DST and midnight-crossing would be rediscovered and got wrong differently). `deferred` says whether the shift moved it, and `deferred_to` is the quiet window's end when it did.

`target_kind` is `personal_event` or `saved_event`. A target that does not exist, is not yours, or is of the other kind is a **404** — never a 403, which would confirm that the record exists.
get.summary: One event's Reminder Plan, with each slot's delivery time

put.description:
Replaces the signed-in user's Reminder Plan for one event with the given slots, and **reschedules the event's pending reminders in the same transaction** — a plan saved without its sends changing is a plan that does nothing.

**0 to 4 slots**, and at most one custom slot. **An empty list is a valid save** and not a delete: it means 'no reminders, but I still see this event in the digest'. The plan row survives, so 'the user chose no reminders' stays distinguishable from 'the user never configured a plan'.

**A custom slot's id carries its offset**: `custom:90` is 90 minutes before the event. The bound is **15 minutes to 30 days** before the event — an offset outside that range is refused.

The response is the saved plan, with each slot's computed delivery time, exactly as the `GET` returns it. A target that does not exist, is not yours, or is of the other kind is a **404** — never a 403, which would confirm that the record exists.

get.description:
The Quiet Hours window, the default Reminder Plan, and the digest delivery time and zone — **in one response**.

**The settings live in two places, and you do not have to care.** The window and the default plan are stored with the delivery service; the delivery time and the zone are stored with the digest service. This endpoint assembles them so the settings screen is one call.

`quiet_hours` is **two local wall clocks** in your own timezone, not instants — `22:00` to `08:00` is the night wherever you are. It is `null` when you have turned quiet hours off, and that is the only way to say so.

`digest.delivery_time` is likewise a **local wall clock** — `09:00` means nine in the morning where you are — and `digest.timezone` is the IANA zone it is a clock in.
get.summary: The signed-in user's notification settings

put.description:
Saves the settings the request mentions, and **re-times the pending reminders and digests in the same transaction** — a setting that does not change what is already scheduled is a setting that does nothing.

**This is a patch.** Every field is optional, and an **omitted field is left alone**: changing your quiet hours does not clear your default plan, and moving your delivery time does not reset your window. The one field where `null` means something is `quiet_hours` — **omit it to leave the window alone, send `null` to turn quiet hours off.**

**The quiet-hours window is two local wall clocks.** A window that covers the whole day (the same clock twice) is refused, because that is the absence of a window rather than a window, and "off" already has one spelling.

**The default Reminder Plan is 0 to 4 slots**, validated by exactly the same rule as a per-event plan — the same named reminders, the same custom-reminder grammar, the same errors. An empty list is valid and means "new reminders start with none". **Changing it does not change plans that already exist**: it applies to events saved from now on.

**The delivery time and the zone are one setting.** A wall clock without its zone is not a schedule, so they are sent together and are applied together.
put.summary: Save the signed-in user's notification settings

get.description:
Every source in the registry, grouped by how its facts were obtained — Official, Community, Aggregator, Crawled — with each source's trust and the caller's mute state.

**The groups are the Source Badge types.** The server names the type; the client owns the label and the glyph.

**A muted source is still listed.** The screen's job is transparency — the user is told what is informing their timeline *and* what they have turned off. A muted source that disappeared would be a preference they could not see or undo.
get.summary: The source registry, grouped, with the caller's visibility settings

post.description:
Reset every source to its default visibility, clearing both the mutes and the "show less" preferences in one action.

**The screen asks before it calls this.** The endpoint is a single idempotent delete; the confirmation belongs to the client, because the safeguard is that the destructive action is confirmed before it completes.

put.description:
Set one source's state to `mute`, `show_less` or `default`.

**`mute` excludes the source's events** — they are not shown at all. **`show_less` deprioritises them** — they are still shown, but ordered lower. **`default` restores the source** to how it was before any preference.

The state is idempotent: setting a source to the state it already has is a success, and `changed` says whether anything actually moved.

**There is no 404.** The endpoint does not read the catalog (AD-3), so a source that is not in the registry is accepted like any other: the preference excludes nothing and is purged with the user's data.

get.description:
Every category the caller has muted, with the server's label for each and when the mute ends.

**A null `expires_at` means the mute is indefinite** — the mockup's "until I change it".

**An expired mute is not in the list.** The row is still there — it is the caller's data — but it no longer mutes anything.
get.summary: The caller's muted categories

put.description:
Mute one category for the caller, for 7, 30 or 90 days — or indefinitely, by sending a null `duration_days`.

**The duration set is closed.** A mute that outlived the caller's patience by a typo is a mute they have to find a screen to undo, so anything else is a 422.

**The mute is idempotent.** Setting a mute that is already set is a success, and `changed` says whether the expiry actually moved.

**The expiry runs from now, not from the mute's creation.** Asking for 30 days again refreshes the window, which is what pressing the button again means.

post.description:
Clear every category mute in one action.

**The screen asks before it calls this.** The endpoint is a single idempotent delete; the confirmation belongs to the client, because the safeguard is that the destructive action is confirmed before it completes.

delete.description:
Unmute one category. One tap, and the row is gone.

**Unmuting does not resurrect the muted events.** The events that were excluded from a digest are excluded from the digests they were excluded from; the next digest is composed from the current candidate pool. A caller who unmutes is asking for the category back *from now on*.

post.description: Verify, translate and apply one inbound billing event.
